prompt: The Eco7 case opinion question asks students to recommend mainly:
options: Launch pricing, distribution, and whether Aventage stores should receive exclusivity
A national Super Bowl advertising campaign only
A merger between Avellin and Sevoline
A new auction format for motor oil distributors
explanation: The prompt asks how Eco7 should be priced, how it affects wholesalers and DIFM stores, how it should be distributed, and whether Aventage stores should receive exclusivity.
reviewHint: Frame the case around price, channel incentives, and exclusivity.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf p.7
prompt: Eco7's strongest positioning is that it combines:
options: Environmental benefits with performance comparable to a synthetic blend
The lowest possible price with no performance claim
A pure DIY-only offer with no installer role
A private-label identity with no Avellin brand support
explanation: Eco7 is made from recycled oil, uses less production energy, and offers longevity/performance comparable to a synthetic blend.
reviewHint: Do not position Eco7 as only green; the case also emphasizes performance.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf pp.3, 10
prompt: Which fact most supports focusing Eco7 on the DIFM channel?
options: Professional service providers were the most influential information source for green motor oil decisions
DIY consumers never care about brand familiarity
National retailers already agreed to promote Eco7 exclusively
Eco7 required no explanation from installers
explanation: The case survey reports professional service providers as the most influential information source, and DIFM buyers often accept installer recommendations.
reviewHint: Connect channel choice to who influences the consumer at the moment of purchase.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf p.8
prompt: The main downside of pricing Eco7 at the lower $5.25 price is that it:
options: Squeezes margins and may undermine premium positioning
Makes the product more expensive than Avellin's synthetic oil
Eliminates all sales in stores with weak messaging
Prevents installers from selling any conventional oil
explanation: The case says $5.25 makes selling easier but squeezes everyone’s margins and may devalue the innovation.
reviewHint: Separate unit sales from profit per sale and positioning effects.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf p.8
prompt: At the $6.75 full price, Eco7 is most likely to sell well when:
options: DIFM installers understand and explain both the green benefit and performance benefit
Installers avoid mentioning the product's environmental benefit
The product is sold only as a cheap substitute for private label
All displays and installer messages are removed
explanation: Test-market feedback said installers who knew how to pitch Eco7 had no problem selling it at full price.
reviewHint: Full-price strategy depends on channel training and message execution.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf p.10
prompt: For a 5-quart oil change, the DIFM outlet gross margin on Eco7 at full price is closest to:
explanation: Eco7 full-price retail revenue is $33.75 per oil change and the DIFM outlet gross margin is 55%, so margin is about $18.56.
reviewHint: Use retail revenue per oil change times outlet gross margin percentage.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf p.10
prompt: For a 5-quart Eco7 oil change at the discounted price, the wholesaler gross margin is closest to:
explanation: At the discounted price, the DIFM outlet cost is $13.125 and the wholesaler margin is 10% of that selling price, or about $1.31.
reviewHint: Work backward from DIFM retail revenue and outlet margin to wholesaler selling price.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf pp.6, 8, 11
prompt: The strongest argument for giving Aventage stores Eco7 exclusivity is that exclusivity could:
options: Increase store commitment and improve execution of the premium message
Guarantee immediate national DIY coverage
Eliminate the need for installer training
Make national mass merchandisers promote Avellin over private label
explanation: The case suggests Aventage stores value exclusivity and may execute the rollout better because they are already engaged with Avellin.
reviewHint: Tie exclusivity to incentives, training, and consistency at the point of sale.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf pp.6, 8
prompt: Why did Avellin consider keeping Eco7 out of national mass merchandisers and clubs at launch?
options: To gain DIFM installer support and limit channel conflict with independent customers
Because DIY consumers were the only target for Eco7
Because national retailers had no PCMO sales
Because AvellinAuto stores required wholesaler distribution
explanation: Avellin planned to focus on independent DIFM and AvellinAuto, partly to support DIFM installers and avoid conflicts with low-cost national channels.
reviewHint: Review how channel decisions change retailer incentives and loyalty.

source: Eco7- Launching a New Motor Oil.pdf pp.7-8
prompt: The test market revealed that Eco7 sales depended heavily on:
options: In-store displays and installer recommendations
National TV awareness alone
DIY shoppers reading technical reports online
Wholesalers avoiding all sales incentives
explanation: Most buyers became aware through displays or DIFM installer suggestions, while relatively few reported seeing local advertising.
reviewHint: For Eco7, the selling message happens inside the service channel.

prompt: Which action was identified as a positive aspect of United's response?
options: United reached out directly to Carroll after the video went viral
United ignored the incident completely
United sued Carroll immediately
United publicly denied that any service failure occurred
explanation: The opinion notes direct outreach as a positive sign that United recognized the situation required attention beyond a routine claim.
reviewHint: Distinguish positive response elements from the larger timing failure.

prompt: The biggest criticism of United's response timing was that:
options: United engaged only after millions had already watched the video
United apologized before Carroll complained
United resolved the complaint within one day
United announced changes before the incident occurred
explanation: The response came after nine months of unresolved complaint attempts and after the video had already gone viral.
reviewHint: In service recovery, delay can become part of the failure.

prompt: Why did United's compensation offer look insufficient from a reputation perspective?
options: It appeared to come only after viral pressure rather than from accountability
It was paired with immediate public operational changes
It prevented the video from spreading at all
It was made before any public criticism
explanation: The opinion argues that acting only under viral pressure signals that customers matter mainly when complaints become PR problems.
reviewHint: Separate private settlement from public trust repair.

prompt: Why was a private outreach to Carroll not enough once the incident became global?
options: A public apology was needed to address broader reputational damage and reassure travelers
The public had no awareness of the incident
Public statements always make service failures disappear
Only legal threats could repair the brand
explanation: Once the case became a public conversation, the response also needed a public trust-building component.
reviewHint: Match the response arena to the damage arena: public harm often needs public repair.

prompt: A stronger United response would have paired an apology with:
options: Specific operational changes such as clearer baggage accountability or complaint timelines
A demand that Carroll remove the video before any discussion
No acknowledgement of the damaged guitar
A promise to handle complaints only when they go viral
explanation: The opinion recommends a public commitment to concrete improvements so customers have evidence of genuine change.
reviewHint: Good service recovery includes apology, accountability, and evidence of system improvement.
